newsitem.title: FRANCE: France takes cautious view on defence shake-up.
newsitem.headline: France takes cautious view on defence shake-up.

text.p: New French Defence Minister Alain Richard said on Thursday he would not be rushed into decisions on a consolidation of the defence industry launched by the previous government.

Richard inherited two sensitive files from the conservative government when he took over his ministry -- the merger and subsequent privatisation of aircraft companies Dassault Aviation and Aerospatiale, and the sell-off of defence electronics firm Thomson-CSF.

"If it was so urgent then it's not urgent any more," Richard told reporters at his first appearance at the weekly ministry briefing. He said people had been talking about restructuring the defence industry for years.

"This is not something you do three times in a row," Richard said. "The key word is 'negotation,' he added. He said he would negotiate with the companies, European allies, labour and management, and the regional authorities.

Budget cuts, required to trim France's public deficits, and U.S. aerospace mega-mergers, are forcing a rationalisation of France's fragmented industry. The conservative administration responded with the Thomson-CSF privatisation and merging state-owned Aerospatiale and privately-owned Dassault.
Telecommunications group Alcatel Alsthom and the Lagardere group have submitted rival bids for the state's 58 percent stake in Thomson-CSF but those firm offers lapse in September.
Richard was quoted as saying there was room for just one plane-maker in Europe and that he saw a combined Dassault-Aerospatiale as simply a component of such a firm.

In testimony to the National Assembly Committee on Defence delivered on Wednesday and made public a day later, Richard added that the situation was different for defence electronics firm Thomson-CSF, which he said was important enough not to have to be submerged into a conglomerate.
"In the aerospace industry, it seems a given that there is room for just one plane-maker, civilian and military, in Europe," Richard told the assembly panel.
"Negotiations in search of agreements with the governments of other countries are fundamental, with the bringing together of Dassault and Aerospatiale a simple component," he said.
But in the defence electronics sector, he said it was not clear that just a single European firm was required.
"The position occupied by Thomson-CSF makes it big enough not to have to be a secondary player," he said.
Dassault makes combat planes, while Aerospatiale derives some 70 percent of its revenues from making commercial jets for the Airbus Industrie consortium.
Richard said in his testimony the new government, swept into power in a June 1 parliamentary election, might have to revise the 1997 defence budget but would not know for a few months.
He said the government had undertaken a budgetary review "which will be presented at the end of the summer and might entail some adjustments".

Budgetary changes might also be dictated by changes in strategic policy over the next five years, he added. If budget changes were required, he pledged that any plans would be fully and openly debated beforehand.
